papers.title: Cost Aware Best Arm Identification
papers.venue: Reinforcement Learning Journal 4 / Reinforcement Learning Conference 2024, pp. 1533-1545
papers.source_type: peer-reviewed conference journal article; official proceedings page with paper and supplement
papers.core_contribution: Defines cost-aware best-arm identification (CABAI), where arms have separate reward and stochastic cost distributions, derives an information-theoretic lower bound, and gives CTAS plus a cheaper Chernoff Overlap allocation rule.
papers.methodology: Fixed-confidence pure exploration; CTAS tracks the optimizer of a cost-normalized Chernoff information problem, while Chernoff Overlap applies a square-root allocation rule and is analyzed exactly for simplified two-arm models.
papers.key_results_location: Official abstract states asymptotic optimality of CTAS and two-arm optimality of Chernoff Overlap but gives no single numerical benchmark delta; detailed theory is in the linked paper.
papers.limitations: Optimizes expected identification cost under fixed confidence, not a hard wall-clock deadline or a joint tail probability. Cost/reward stationarity and repeated-sampling assumptions do not automatically hold across heterogeneous model/guardrail replay cells.
papers.motivation: Testing actions can have very different costs even when deployment reward is the true objective.
constraints_inferred: A candidate family needs measurable reward and cost samples.
A fixed-confidence objective must be translated into the competition's score and void-risk target.
Replay multiplicity must be included in each arm's effective cost.
key_decisions: Allocate exploration by information gained per expected cost.
Use a low-complexity square-root rule only after validating its simplified-model assumptions.
tried_and_discarded: Cost-oblivious best-arm allocation, shown to be suboptimal when action costs differ.
load_bearing_assumptions: Arm cost and reward distributions are sufficiently stable to estimate.
Expected-cost optimality is an acceptable proxy unless augmented with a tail constraint.
papers.relevance_reason: Direct template for deciding which candidate families deserve scarce generation/evaluation effort before returning a replayed portfolio.

papers.title: On Stochastic Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks in Small Budget Regime
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an adaptive universal primal-dual method for contextual bandits with stochastic reward/cost vectors when the resource budget is small.
papers.methodology: Primal-dual online learning with budget-aware control, Lyapunov drift analysis, and refined cumulative-variance bounds; handles regimes with and without strict feasibility information.
papers.key_results: For B = Omega(sqrt(T)), AUPD obtains tilde-O((1 + nu*/(delta b)) sqrt(T)) regret under strict feasibility and tilde-O(sqrt(T) + (nu*/sqrt(b)) T^(3/4)) without strict feasibility, where b=B/T.
papers.key_results_location: Official ICLR abstract; the two bounds are stated as results (i) and (ii).
papers.limitations: Regret is cumulative expectation, not an explicit deadline-miss probability. The sequential contextual protocol differs from one-shot candidate generation followed by mandatory replay. Constants hidden by tilde-O can dominate at competition scale.
papers.motivation: Online systems must learn rewards while respecting scarce, consumable resources even when the budget is only order sqrt(T).
constraints_inferred: Maintain an explicit resource ledger.
Include a no-op or safe fallback action to preserve feasibility.
Budget slack delta b is a first-class control parameter.
key_decisions: Update shadow prices as budget is consumed.
Prefer a universal policy when the feasibility margin is not known.
tried_and_discarded: Large-budget analyses that require B much larger than sqrt(T).
Policies requiring prior knowledge of the strict-feasibility margin.
load_bearing_assumptions: Stochastic contexts/costs follow the paper's model.
Budget consumption is observable after each action.
A safe null action is available.
papers.relevance_reason: Gives an online allocation architecture and explicit safety-margin role when evidence must be gathered under a tight total execution budget.

papers.title: Hiring Under Uncertainty
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019, pp. 5181-5189
papers.source_type: peer-reviewed conference paper; official PMLR proceedings
papers.core_contribution: Models value-maximizing selection under uncertain acceptance and a hard time limit, including sequential, parallel, and stochastic-knapsack-with-finite-probes variants.
papers.methodology: Approximation algorithms choose offer/probe schedules from candidate values, acceptance probabilities, deadlines, and finite probing constraints.
papers.key_results: Provides a 2-approximation for sequential offers, an 8-approximation for parallel offers, and a 10-approximation for the more general stochastic knapsack setting with finite probes.
papers.limitations: The uncertainty is candidate acceptance timing rather than model latency, and the approximation objective is expected value rather than a calibrated upper bound on deadline failure. Independence and distributional assumptions need rechecking for correlated replay cells.
papers.motivation: A decision maker must maximize acquired value before a deadline when each attempted item may fail or consume uncertain time.
constraints_inferred: Distinguish sequential generation probes from the later parallel or repeated replay cost.
Candidate value must be portfolio-marginal, not merely standalone.
A hard return deadline changes the optimal number of probes.
key_decisions: Choose sequential versus parallel policy using the actual evaluation protocol.
Account for finite probes explicitly instead of assuming unlimited retries.
load_bearing_assumptions: Acceptance/latency distributions are known or estimable.
The modeled deadline semantics match the evaluator's treatment of unfinished work.
papers.relevance_reason: Closest reviewed analogue to selecting a valuable finite batch whose uncertain processing must finish before a deadline.

papers.title: Approximating the Stochastic Knapsack Problem: The Benefit of Adaptivity
papers.venue: Mathematics of Operations Research 33(4), 2008; conference version FOCS 2004
papers.core_contribution: Formalizes stochastic knapsack with deterministic values and independent random sizes, comparing adaptive policies against fixed nonadaptive orderings.
papers.methodology: Sequential packing with size revealed only after insertion; constructs polynomial-time nonadaptive and adaptive approximation policies and analyzes the adaptivity gap.
papers.key_results: A polynomial-time nonadaptive policy achieves expected value within a factor of 4 of the optimal adaptive policy.
papers.limitations: Assumes independent item sizes with known distributions and maximizes expected completed value; it does not provide a user-chosen probability of meeting the deadline. The final overflowing item loses value, which may not match a competition-wide void on timeout.
papers.motivation: Random job times make a fixed portfolio/order potentially less valuable than a policy that reacts to realized remaining time.
constraints_inferred: If generation truly happens once, use the nonadaptive-policy results as the closer analogue.
If the evaluator voids the whole result on timeout, strengthen the loss model beyond final-item overflow.
Correlated replay latencies violate the independence premise.
key_decisions: Estimate whether adaptivity is operationally available.
Reserve capacity for stochastic overruns rather than filling to mean size.
tried_and_discarded: Treating random item sizes as deterministic means.
load_bearing_assumptions: Item execution sizes are independent.
Distributions are known.
Expected value, not chance-constrained feasibility, is the governing objective.
papers.relevance_reason: Foundational model for choosing valuable candidates with uncertain replay times under a single total deadline.

papers.title: Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
papers.core_contribution: Learns the distribution of response reward as a function of input and compute budget, then allocates best-of-k samples or expensive routing selectively to hard-but-solvable inputs.
papers.methodology: Predicts reward distributions for input-budget pairs and optimizes computation across a batch; evaluated for adaptive best-of-k reranking and cheap-versus-expensive decoding routes.
papers.key_results: Reduces computation by up to 50% at no loss in response quality, or improves quality by up to 10% at a fixed compute budget.
papers.limitations: Optimizes compute and quality, not a wall-clock chance constraint. Reward predictors trained on benchmark tasks may not transfer to hidden target models or security guardrails; constructed response profiles cannot confirm target response heterogeneity.
papers.motivation: Uniform inference compute wastes effort on easy or impossible cases and starves hard but solvable cases.
constraints_inferred: Calibrate a utility-versus-budget curve per candidate family.
Include generation, verification, and tool overhead in compute accounting.
Do not infer hidden-cell utility from a simulator without uncertainty bounds.
key_decisions: Spend marginal compute where predicted reward gain is largest.
Stop allocating to likely impossible cases.
tried_and_discarded: Uniform best-of-k allocation across all inputs.
load_bearing_assumptions: Reward distributions can be learned from representative data.
The reward model is sufficiently calibrated under target shift.
Compute units are comparable across decoding choices.
papers.relevance_reason: Direct evidence for replacing uniform generation effort with marginal-value allocation across candidate families.

papers.title: Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute: A Bandit Learning Approach
papers.source_type: peer-reviewed conference paper; arXiv primary manuscript
papers.core_contribution: Frames allocation of a fixed test-time compute budget across queries as fully adaptive pure-exploration bandit learning, estimating difficulty online and prioritizing solvable hard queries.
papers.methodology: Sequentially samples query arms, estimates their difficulty from observed intermediate outcomes, and reallocates remaining compute to maximize the number answered correctly under a fixed total budget.
papers.key_results: Reports up to 11.10 percentage points improvement (15.04% relative) on MATH-500 and up to 7.41 percentage points (14.40% relative) on LiveCodeBench.
papers.limitations: Assumes informative intermediate correctness signals and adaptive per-query sampling, unlike a strict one-shot generation protocol. It targets answer count, not deadline tail risk, and may overfit benchmark-specific process rewards.
papers.motivation: A fixed batch budget should not be divided uniformly across heterogeneous query difficulties.
constraints_inferred: Only use online reallocations available before the single returned portfolio is frozen.
Treat candidate families as arms only if feedback is observable during local validation.
Add a separate feasibility guard for remote deadline risk.
key_decisions: Prioritize hard but still solvable arms.
Cease spending on already solved or apparently unsolvable arms.
tried_and_discarded: Two-stage policies requiring a separately trained allocator when online feedback suffices.
load_bearing_assumptions: Intermediate feedback correlates with final utility.
Query difficulty is learnable within the available budget.
Local query population resembles evaluation demand.
papers.relevance_reason: Offers a direct adaptive-bandit abstraction for allocating scarce local generation/evaluation compute before submission.

papers.title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
papers.source_type: peer-reviewed conference paper; official author/company research page with public code link
papers.core_contribution: Reframes reasoning-budget selection as distribution-free risk control and calibrates upper and lower stopping thresholds to a user-selected error risk while minimizing compute.
papers.methodology: Uses held-out calibration data and distribution-free risk control to set a confidence upper stop and a parametric lower stop for likely-unsolvable instances; an efficiency loss selects among multiple risk-valid stopping rules.
papers.key_results_location: Official Apple research abstract states that experiments adhere to user-specified risk targets but gives no single exact aggregate reduction; code is linked there.
papers.limitations: The guarantee concerns reasoning error under calibration assumptions, not the probability that a replay portfolio finishes before a wall-clock deadline. Marginal rather than conditional guarantees may be insufficient under severe cell shift or dependence.
papers.motivation: Stopping thresholds are otherwise uninterpretable knobs with an unmanaged accuracy-compute tradeoff.
constraints_inferred: Set an explicit void-risk target before choosing portfolio size.
Calibrate on exchangeable, representative replay traces.
Use a joint deadline loss if failure of any replay cell voids the portfolio.
key_decisions: Choose risk tolerance first, then minimize compute among calibrated policies.
Use both success and futility stopping rules when online adaptation is permitted.
tried_and_discarded: A token budget chosen without mapping to an interpretable risk.
load_bearing_assumptions: Calibration and deployment examples are exchangeable or adequately weighted.
The loss function exactly matches the operational failure event.
The calibration set is large enough for the chosen risk level.
papers.relevance_reason: Best direct source for converting an arbitrary safety margin into an explicit, calibrated risk target, though the loss must be redefined for deadlines.

papers.title: Scheduling LLM Inference with Uncertainty-Aware Output Length Predictions
papers.core_contribution: Models stochastic LLM output length with a heavy-tailed log-t distribution and replaces point-estimate shortest-job-first priority with a tail-inflated expectation using CVaR-style tail sensitivity.
papers.methodology: Fits an output-length distribution rather than a point forecast, derives Tail Inflated Expectation (TIE), and evaluates online scheduling and offline data-generation workloads against three baselines.
papers.key_results: TIE reduces per-token latency by 2.31x for online inference and improves throughput by 1.42x for offline data generation.
papers.limitations: Recent unreviewed preprint; throughput and per-token latency are not deadline-completion probabilities. A log-t marginal fit does not capture cross-cell dependence, shared queue shocks, or mandatory replay multiplication.
papers.motivation: Point output-length estimates underprice rare long generations and cause head-of-line blocking.
constraints_inferred: Fit tails, not only means or observed maxima.
Model the sum or maximum induced by the actual replay topology.
Stress shared shocks and dependence rather than multiplying independent marginals.
key_decisions: Rank work by a tail-inflated cost proxy.
Use CVaR-like penalties as diagnostics, then enforce a separate deadline chance constraint for safety.
tried_and_discarded: Point-estimate SJF as the sole uncertainty treatment.
load_bearing_assumptions: Log-t adequately fits target output lengths.
Historical traces represent the target serving regime.
Scheduler overhead and GPU-memory effects remain secondary.
papers.relevance_reason: Strong latency-tail diagnostic for LLM execution, but it optimizes serving order rather than selecting a one-shot replay portfolio with a hard void deadline.

papers.title: Probabilistic Partial Set Covering with an Oracle for Chance Constraints
papers.source_type: peer-reviewed journal article; publisher DOI page
papers.core_contribution: Formulates binary subset selection with an explicit risk level epsilon and a probability oracle enforcing that a desired coverage event occurs with probability at least 1-epsilon.
papers.methodology: Combines an exact probability oracle with a compact mixed-integer formulation in a special case; for large instances, couples sampling with oracle-based feasibility checking/fixing and facet-defining inequalities from a submodular structure.
papers.key_results_location: Publisher abstract reports exact and sampling-based solution methods but no single exact benchmark number.
papers.limitations: Requires an exact probability oracle under specified coverage distributions for its strongest feasibility claims. The portfolio objective is minimum cost to reach probabilistic coverage, not maximum security score under uncertain replay duration.
papers.motivation: Expected performance alone cannot enforce that a discrete portfolio meets a reliability target.
constraints_inferred: Define the deadline event computationally as total replay time <= 9000 seconds.
Use epsilon as the explicit acceptable void probability.
Validate and repair any sampled solution against a higher-fidelity tail/dependence oracle.
key_decisions: Separate objective maximization from probabilistic feasibility.
Use sampling for search but an oracle or conservative bound for final feasibility certification.
tried_and_discarded: Accepting a sample-average feasible portfolio without probability-oracle checking.
load_bearing_assumptions: The probability oracle is correct for the joint execution-cost distribution.
The event and all binary selection semantics are completely specified.
Sampling error is controlled before accepting feasibility.
papers.relevance_reason: Supplies the cleanest discrete chance-constraint pattern for an explicit deadline-void target and a selected returned set.

papers.title: Robust Submodular Observation Selection
papers.venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research 9, 2008, pp. 2761-2801
papers.source_type: peer-reviewed journal article; official JMLR page
papers.core_contribution: Develops SATURATE for maximizing worst-case value across multiple monotone submodular objectives, with extensions to nonunit, communication, and path costs and to mean/worst-case tradeoffs.
papers.methodology: Binary-searches a saturation threshold and greedily covers truncated submodular objectives; bicriteria relaxation permits logarithmic budget expansion to obtain the robust objective value.
papers.key_results: For integral objectives, Theorem 5 returns A with min_i F_i(A) at least the size-k optimum while allowing |A| <= alpha k, where alpha = 1 + ln(max_s sum_i F_i({s})); Theorem 3 shows no polynomial-time multiplicative approximation at exact cardinality unless P=NP.
papers.key_results_location: Paper Sections 3-5, specifically Theorems 3 and 5 on the official JMLR PDF linked from the article page.
papers.limitations: The robust objective assumes each cell-specific utility is monotone submodular and usually needs a logarithmic budget violation. It does not model stochastic latency tails or give a chance constraint; exact-cardinality robust maximization is strongly inapproximable.
papers.motivation: A portfolio should remain useful under several plausible objectives/environments rather than maximize average value in one environment.
constraints_inferred: Treat model/guardrail cells as separate objectives only after verifying approximate diminishing returns.
Do not assume simulator diversity proves target response heterogeneity.
Combine robust utility selection with a separate joint latency chance constraint.
key_decisions: Optimize worst-cell marginal coverage when robustness is more important than average score.
Reject bicriteria expansion if the replay deadline budget cannot be violated.
tried_and_discarded: Naive greedy optimization of the nonsubmodular min_i F_i objective at exact cardinality.
load_bearing_assumptions: Each cell utility is normalized, monotone, and submodular or close enough for the heuristic.
A logarithmic cost/cardinality relaxation is operationally acceptable for the guarantee.
Enumerated objectives cover the relevant deployment cells.
papers.relevance_reason: Useful for diversifying a replay portfolio across cells, but its bicriteria guarantee and lack of latency modeling limit direct use under a hard deadline.
